observations.quote: But the more single and subtle part of the Galenists, who like Nicodemus are of a milder temper
observations.what: the more single and subtle part of the Galenists
observations.note: One part of the Galenists is set apart and likened to Nicodemus; the paragraph opens with a printed 3, and the earlier members of that run are not in the lines given.

observations.quote: for fear of being excommunicated by some Athenian Rabbies, durst not openly professe the truth
observations.note: This milder part of the Galenists holds back from professing the truth for fear of persons called Athenian Rabbies; the lines given do not say who these are.

observations.quote: these with open Arms will most readily imbrace this so long look't for, and desired light
observations.note: Croll expects this milder part to welcome what he brings, which he calls a light long looked for.

observations.quote: Envy which will certainly arise from hence, should grieve and be troubled that these things should be made common for publick use
observations.note: Croll presents these things as being made common for publick use and foresees that envy will be troubled by exactly that.

observations.quote: When envy and hatred give counsell, the Judgement is nothing worth.
observations.note: Margin maxim beside the foreseen ill omen: a judgement counselled by envy and hatred is worthless.

observations.quote: they will a little coldly commend those things, which notwithstanding are secretly reserved for their uses
observations.note: The envious are foreseen to praise coldly in the open what they secretly keep for their own use.

observations.quote: though (to such) without Gods blessing upon them
observations.note: Croll holds that the things so reserved are without God's blessing for such users.

observations.quote: virtue can never be found without the marks and wounds of envy
observations.note: Croll holds that envy always accompanies virtue and those who desire the good of a Common-wealth.

observations.quote: I study not to please all, for neither all men nor all things please me.
observations.note: A first-person saying in the margin beside the passage on envy: he does not aim to please all. Margin notes are the author's own and this one names no other speaker.

observations.quote: the hardest matter that can be, to doe an acceptable work to an ingratefull world
observations.note: Croll calls the world ungrateful and his work hard to make acceptable to it; he adds that the envious deserve pity rather than envy.

observations.quote: till in good time they willingly deliver themselves out of the Purgatory of their own malice
observations.note: Purgatory is a figure whose sense the text states: the Purgatory of their own malice, which torments them.

observations.quote: As for the more dull and drossie sort of them
observations.what: the more dull and drossie sort of them
observations.note: A second sort is set apart from the milder part of OPEN.12: those who reject the truth and take error for their Companion.

observations.quote: these will angrily challenge and provoke this my good endeavour toward the publick, with most scornfull reproaches
observations.note: Croll calls his work a good endeavour toward the publick and expects scornful reproaches for it from this sort.

observations.quote: according to the Comaedian, there can be nothing more unjust then these leud haters of Chymistry, and despisers of wisdome
observations.name: Comaedian
observations.note: A judgement of injustice is given on the authority of 'the Comaedian', not named further in the lines given, and applied to the haters of Chymistry.

observations.quote: being plunged into Scholasticall dirt and dust over head and ears
observations.note: Croll describes the dull opponents as sunk in school learning.

observations.quote: had rather dye in their old tract, and grosse folly, then be thought to learn of those whose Masters they accounted themselves to be
observations.note: These men would rather die in their old way than be seen to learn from those they counted their pupils.

observations.quote: There is a two-fold Alchymy. Naturall, much esteemed by Artist. Sophisticall, as much detested by them.
observations.what: a two-fold Alchymy
observations.note: The margin divides Alchymy into two, Naturall and Sophisticall, the one esteemed and the other detested by those it calls Artist.

observations.quote: these insolent and open contemners of Natures secrets, who tremble at the very name of Chymistry
observations.note: The opponents are called contemners of Natures secrets who fear the very name of Chymistry; Nature is said to have secrets, and Chymistry is named in the same breath.

observations.quote: shamelesly to scoff at this Divine Art
observations.what: this Divine Art
observations.note: Chymistry is named a Divine Art.

observations.quote: whereas they never yet so much as saluted it at the threshold
observations.note: The revilers abuse an art they have never so much as approached.

observations.quote: trample upon the Truth, and those Pearls cast before them
observations.note: Pearls is a figure. Interpreted: the Pearls are what is offered to these men together with the Truth, something precious given to those who cannot value it, since both are trampled in the one phrase; the lines given say no more.

observations.quote: their Captain, that railing Binarius
observations.what: that railing Binarius
observations.note: The opponents' only weapons come from a Captain named Binarius; the lines given do not say who or what is meant by the name.

observations.quote: there is no other reason why it should be sent to the Isle Anticyra
observations.note: Their rage and Cyclopean fury is to be sent to the Isle Anticyra; the phrase is figurative and the lines given do not say what the place stands for.

observations.quote: their ignorance of the just and due preparation of things
observations.note: Croll gives the opponents' ignorance of the right preparation of things as the one reason of their fury, and claims they themselves will confess it; the confession is his claim, not words given to them.

observations.quote: to determine of those as if we were well acquainted with them, is not only foolish, but filthy
observations.note: Croll holds that to judge unknown things as if known is foolish and filthy.

observations.quote: such Scholastick Doctors, who for want of wit could never find the way into Natures Sanctuary
observations.note: Nature is spoken of as having a Sanctuary into which the Scholastick Doctors never found the way.

observations.quote: doe no lesse then the common people, admire, as Magical Miracles, those eminent works wherein the whole power of Nature flourisheth
observations.what: those eminent works wherein the whole power of Nature flourisheth
observations.note: Certain works are set apart as those in which the whole power of Nature flourishes; Magical Miracles is how the convinced Doctors admire them, like the common people, not Croll's own name for them.

observations.quote: many famous Phisitians of our time, equall to the most learned of men, who have spent all their life in the works of Art, men skill'd in the secrets of Nature
observations.what: the secrets of Nature
observations.note: The physicians Croll defends against the Doctors are praised as spent in the works of Art and skilled in the secrets of Nature.

observations.quote: John 5.44.
observations.name: John
observations.note: A margin note naming a writing by chapter and verse, set where the text turns to the Honours of the world these physicians have not taken.

observations.quote: they have not taken upon them those most vain Honours of the world
observations.note: Croll calls the academic honours most vain; these physicians are condemned for not having taken them.

observations.quote: See Paracels. Tom. 5. in fragm. Medicis. fol. 167, 168.
observations.name: Paracels.
observations.note: The note sends the reader to a named place in a writing of Paracels. beside the passage on honours and titles, then goes on against binding students to set authors; the text does not show whether those sentences are Paracels.'s or Croll's.

observations.quote: It is a wicked Tyranny to captivate the fancy of Students to certain Authors, and take away the freedome of finding out and following the truth from young Scholars.
observations.note: The note condemns binding students to certain authors; it follows the reference to Paracels. and does not show whose sentence it is.

observations.quote: Money and Friends advance more then desert.
observations.note: Advancement goes by money and friends more than by desert; the same note, after the reference to Paracels.

observations.quote: (as they call them) the Authorities and Titles of Doctorship
observations.name: they
observations.note: The names Authorities and Titles of Doctorship are given as the Doctors' own words for the honours; a gap of one illegible letter follows the last word.

observations.quote: with which neither Hippocrates nor Galen, nor any Phisitians that we read of in their time were indowed or adorned
observations.note: Croll argues that Hippocrates and Galen, authentic in the opponents' own opinion, bore no such titles.

observations.quote: least they should be made to swear to the Heathenish errors of the School-Gods, against the naked Truth, and be bound by an Academicall Oath, to live and dye in them
observations.note: The reason the good physicians refuse the titles: the oath would bind them to what Croll calls the Heathenish errors of the School-Gods.

observations.quote: these personated Titles heretofore by a commendable institution were the spur of virtue, and the deserved reward of Learning
observations.note: Croll grants that the titles were once a commendable institution and a deserved reward.

observations.quote: now adayes, especially in Phisick, they are bestowed either through flattery or bribery
observations.note: Croll holds that the titles are now given, in Phisick above all, by flattery or bribery.

observations.quote: I speak not of those who obtain the true Titles and Bayes of their, Degrees by their deserts in Learning
observations.note: Croll exempts from his charge those who earn their degrees by learning.

observations.quote: they have found the brittlenesse by the losse of so noble a vessel
observations.note: Vessel is not said plainly. Interpreted: the noble vessel lost is the patient's body, since the same sentence goes on to whether the Patient live or die and N026 speaks of man's skin and the Image of God.

observations.quote: proceeding according to their method whereby they excuse all their errors, whether the Patient live or die
observations.note: The titled physicians' method serves to excuse their errors whatever the outcome.

observations.quote: whether Galens Axioms (as he writeth) doe any more concern us, then they doe wild Bears and Bores
observations.name: Galen
observations.note: The comparison with wild Bears and Bores is given as something written ('as he writeth'); Galen is the only person named in the clause, though the lines given do not name the writer outright. It is turned against Galen's own axioms.

observations.quote: whether his Method of Phisick, wherein this Age so much triumpheth, hath any good foundation, being not supported with any Authority of Antiquity
observations.note: They question, and not without cause, whether Galen's Method of Phisick has a foundation; Croll states that it lacks the authority of antiquity.

observations.quote: they are Ocularly convinced that the end doth not answer his beginning in the great Cures of Diseases
observations.note: The ground of the doubt is what they see with their own eyes: in great cures Galen's method does not answer its promise.

observations.quote: The Earth hideth the error of such Physitians
observations.note: The grave covers the errors of such physicians; the same note speaks of their enriching the Church-yard.

observations.quote: as Socrates saith of rash Physitians, sport & play with mans skin
observations.name: Socrates
observations.note: A saying about rash physicians playing with man's skin is given to Socrates; the words 'or rather the Image of God' that follow stand as a correction, and the note does not show whose they are.

observations.quote: the Art of Phisick is so immense and large, that we may well account it as a very great blessing if (which is sufficient) we attain unto it even in the beginning of our old Age
observations.note: Croll holds the Art of Phisick so large that to reach it by the start of old age is a great blessing and enough.

observations.quote: they plead in defence of their sloth and idlenesse, that they need not take any more paines for further knowledge, having the benefit of other mens labours and observations
observations.name: they
observations.note: The physicians' plea, reported by Croll in order to reject it: other men's labours and observations spare them further pains.

observations.quote: they ought to become Schollars and servants, not Doctors and Masters of Nature
observations.note: The physician's place toward Nature is that of scholar and servant; these men will have to begin all anew.

observations.quote: God onely is Lord and Master of Nature
observations.note: The note beside the passage on arrogance: God alone is Master of Nature.

observations.quote: although it may give greater authority in the world, and vaine glorious estimation of a Name
observations.note: A Degree or Title gives worldly authority and the estimation of a name; the words before, on its not making wiser or more learned, hold a gap of two illegible letters.

observations.quote: How many of this sort of Phisitians have come with their gray haires complaining unto me?
observations.note: Croll speaks of his own experience: old physicians of this sort came to him with complaints.

observations.quote: Fooleries are to be forgotten.
observations.note: Margin maxim beside the old physicians' complaint; a gap marked as foreign script follows it.

observations.quote: in the common toyes of School-vanities, and in Phisicall notions, nothing at all availing to the effecting of their cures
observations.note: The school learning in which they spent their time did nothing for their cures.

observations.quote: like those that feed on Crabs and Crevises, they find much shell but little meat
observations.note: Stated: a comparison the text applies itself to the school studies, much shell and little meat.

observations.quote: having first cast away Opinion and Scorne the lets of learning
observations.note: Opinion and Scorne are named as hindrances of learning, cast away before these men came to knowledge of their errors.

observations.quote: The world is ruled by Opinion.
observations.note: Margin maxim beside the casting away of Opinion.

observations.quote: to put off their old skin, like the wise Serpent, and putting on a new one, to become Schollars of Chymistry
observations.note: The change of skin is a figure whose sense the text gives in the same clause (Stated): in old age they became Schollars of Chymistry.

observations.quote: spend the rest of their dayes with those Secrets which are both in God and Nature
observations.what: those Secrets which are both in God and Nature
observations.note: The object of the converts' study of Chymistry is named as Secrets lying both in God and in Nature.

observations.quote: God is the first book that teacheth us eternall life: for the rule of life is from God.
observations.note: The note names God as the first book and says what it teaches: eternall life.

observations.quote: it is a lovely thing for old men to study Wisdome, and with Diogenes, not give over the Race that they are running
observations.note: Croll approves of old men studying Wisdome; Diogenes is named as an example of not giving over the race, but no words are given to him, so the kind is corrected from voice.

observations.quote: next after the great book of Grace, wherein the eternall health of our soules consisteth
observations.what: the great book of Grace
observations.note: A book of Grace is named and placed first; in it the eternal health of souls consists.

observations.quote: more diligently to pry into that other also of Nature, treating of those Secrets which respect our bodily health
observations.what: that other also of Nature
observations.note: A second book, of Nature, is named; it treats of the Secrets that concern bodily health.

observations.quote: those choise treasures of Nature, wherein the most High hath laid up medicines for our greatest and worst diseases
observations.note: Croll holds that the most High has laid up medicines for the worst diseases in treasures of Nature, which are not to be passed by unnoticed.

observations.quote: The firmament or heaven with all therein is the second Naturall book conducing to a mortall life
observations.note: The note says what the second book is: the firmament or heaven with all in it, serving mortal life.

observations.quote: for the knowledge of Phisick is got from the Stars
observations.note: The note gives as its reason that the knowledge of Phisick comes from the Stars.

observations.quote: God is the first book
observations.note: The note names God as the first book, the paragraph names the first book the great book of Grace; likewise N031 names the second the firmament or heaven, the paragraph the book of Nature. The lines given do not say that the two namings are one.

observations.quote: buried in the dead shadows of meer outsides
observations.note: Dead shadows of meer outsides is a figure for what these physicians do not want to die in; set against an inside not named here.

observations.quote: or the externall Galenicall qualities
observations.note: The 'or' joins this phrase to meer outsides just before the note mark: the outsides are named as the external Galenicall qualities.

observations.quote: they have built a stately Structure and a Temple as a most honourable monument to their old age and Nature
observations.note: Interpreted: the building and temple stand for what these old physicians gained as Schollars of Chymistry (OPEN.17), since out of it they obtain knowledge and the fruit of their labours.

observations.quote: unto which they have attained as well by the sedulous search and admiration of the works of God
observations.note: The clearer knowledge of the Creator is reached by searching and admiring the works of God.

observations.quote: by their laborious examination, and Phylosophicall sequestration of the Creatures, or Naturall things
observations.note: Work done on the Creatures, glossed as Naturall things, is named: examination and Phylosophicall sequestration. The lines given name the work but describe no step of it.

observations.quote: this excellent fruit of their labours, watchings, time and experiences
observations.what: this excellent fruit of their labours, watchings, time and experiences
observations.note: A result is announced as one thing, next to the knowledge of the Creator; the viz. that follows says what it is.

observations.quote: That when they shall be sent for to the sick (where not many words to dispute, but much skill to cure availeth most) they may come as well experienced Phisitians
observations.note: The fruit is stated: they come to the sick as experienced physicians; Croll holds that at the sickbed skill to cure counts, not disputing.

observations.quote: not pretending now to study that disease which they intend to patch up with some outward flattering plaister
observations.note: The experienced physician is set against one who only patches a disease outwardly while pretending to study it.

observations.quote: with a multitude of frivolous services, and sugured words to cloak their simplicity
observations.note: The covering is the common physicians' own: services and sweet words cloak their lack of skill.

observations.quote: insinuating into the richer sort for base gaine, but altogether slighting others of meaner fortune
observations.note: Croll charges the common sort of proud physicians with courting the rich for gain and slighting the poor.

observations.quote: The happines of this present life consisteth in the knowledge of Nature
observations.note: The note places the happiness of this life in the knowledge of Nature.

observations.quote: in temporalls the chiefest thing is to find out the secrets of Nature
observations.note: The note ranks finding out the secrets of Nature first among temporal things, next after eternal ones.

observations.quote: One shall not repent of such a Phisitian who hath the true knowledg of earthly things.
observations.note: The note commends the physician who has true knowledge of earthly things; a reference to Agrip: follows, and the note does not show whether the sentence is his or Croll's.

observations.quote: Vid: Agrip: lib. 6. Epist. c.
observations.name: Agrip:
observations.note: The note sends the reader to a named place in a writing of Agrip: beside the praise of the physician who knows earthly things.

observations.quote: the end of Phisick is not to scrape up money, but to discover the secrets of Nature, and the love of the Phisitian to the sick
observations.note: The note says what the end of Phisick is and is not; its opening words hold two gaps of one illegible word each.

observations.quote: every where forbid, as poisonous, those Phisicall Secrets
observations.name: some of this ribble rabble
observations.voice: QUOTED: some of this ribble rabble
observations.note: The judgement poisonous is the opponents', reported by Croll in order to reject it; he himself calls the things Phisicall Secrets.

observations.quote: inventions of (Chymists, which they call) Collier-like-Phisitians
observations.name: some of this ribble rabble
observations.voice: QUOTED: some of this ribble rabble
observations.note: Collier-like-Phisitians is the opponents' name for the Chymists, reported in order to reject it.

observations.quote: they have a secret and subtle desire to learne those things which they hope to use with success and profit
observations.note: The men who forbid these things in public secretly desire to learn and use them.

observations.quote: robbing the Inventers of the Art, and their Benefactours, of their deserved honour by a mendacious and inverted theft
observations.note: Croll charges them with taking the praise due to the true Author of medicines they got by craft.

observations.quote: To these A pule jan Bravadoes, whether they put on the Lyons or the Foxes skin
observations.what: these A pule jan Bravadoes
observations.note: The men just described are given a name, printed A pule jan Bravadoes, and two skins, the Lyons and the Foxes; the lines given do not explain the name.

observations.quote: admission to the Bath of Diana is not to be granted
observations.note: Something called the Bath of Diana is to be kept closed to these men; the lines given do not say what it is.

observations.quote: Pythagoras forbids to put our victualls into a close stool
observations.name: Pythagoras
observations.note: A prohibition credited to Pythagoras is the stated reason for refusing admission; victualls and close stool are applied by the text to what is offered and to those unworthy of it.

observations.quote: nor should we bestow our choicest herbs on such as rudely rush into the Chymists garden, seeing brambles and thistles will serve their turne
observations.note: The choicest herbs of the Chymists garden are to be withheld from rude intruders; garden and herbs are not explained in the lines given.

observations.quote: the calumnies and reproaches of leud and ignorant men are, in the opinion of the wise, not to be regarded by heroike spirits
observations.name: the wise
observations.note: That reproaches of the ignorant are to be disregarded is given as the opinion of the wise.

observations.quote: the flye never falls into the seething pot
observations.note: A saying set beside the disregard of calumnies. Interpreted: the seething pot stands for the heroike spirits and the flye for the revilers, so slander does not touch the heroic; the saying follows directly on them and N035 repeats it.

observations.quote: The boyling pot doth {G014: 1 letter illegible}ot {G015: 1 letter illegible}ear the siege of flies.
observations.note: The note repeats, in other words and with two one-letter gaps, the saying of the pot and the flies in OPEN.21.

observations.quote: the more humane and civill inclinations also of some make me expect better things
observations.note: Croll expects better of some, once hatred of Truth and violent censures are laid aside.

observations.quote: wherewith some have endeavoured to make such gifts of God suspected and hated by poor and rich
observations.note: Croll calls the things censured gifts of God.

observations.quote: would I for the unworthinesse of some shut these doors against those that seek after the true and Ancient Phisick
observations.what: the true and Ancient Phisick
observations.note: Croll will not shut the doors on seekers of the true and Ancient Phisick because of the unworthy; the word before the quote is damaged by a one-letter gap.

observations.quote: give place to Paracelsus according to his desert in practice and preparations
observations.note: Croll holds that Paracelsus deserves his due place in practice and preparations.

observations.quote: admission to the Bath of Diana is not to be granted, because Pythagoras forbids to put our victualls into a close stool
observations.note: Here admission and the choicest herbs are refused to some, while OPEN.12 speaks of these things being made common for publick use; the same paragraph goes on to say the doors are not shut on true seekers.

observations.quote: these things here mentioned in this place, and in these times, may not be at all judged superfluous or beside the matter in hand
observations.note: Croll defends his accusations as fitting the place and the times.

observations.quote: neither will this Discourse offend any holy and Learned Phisitian
observations.note: No holy and learned physician is touched by his Discourse.

observations.quote: which I intend onely against those proud, envious, ignorant vassalls, who oppose the Chymicall verity against conscience
observations.note: Croll limits his attack to those who oppose what he calls the Chymicall verity against their conscience.

observations.quote: before I come to describe the Remedies
observations.note: Points forward to a description of the Remedies to come after what the Preface handles; that description is not in the lines given.

observations.quote: I handle some things in this Admonitary Preface
observations.what: this Admonitary Preface
observations.note: Croll names the present writing, spelled Admonitary here and Admonitory in the heading, and announces the things it handles; the numbered heads follow.

observations.quote: which with greatest intention of mind, and most diligent scruting, are to be explained by a Philosophicall Phisitian
observations.note: These matters are for a Philosophicall Phisitian to explain, with the greatest attention.

observations.quote: What that Phisick is which cureth mens diseases, and few Phisitians know it.
observations.what: What that Phisick is which cureth mens diseases
observations.note: The head numbered I of the things the Preface handles.

observations.quote: and few Phisitians know it
observations.note: The Phisick that cures is said to be known to few physicians.

observations.quote: Whereunto is added a perfect Philosophicall Description of the little World Man, almost forgotten and unknown.
observations.what: a perfect Philosophicall Description of the little World Man
observations.note: A second matter is announced under the same number I, as an addition.

observations.quote: the little World Man
observations.note: The words set little World and Man side by side as names of one thing.

observations.quote: almost forgotten and unknown
observations.note: Several defensible readings: the words may say that the Description is almost forgotten and unknown, or that the little World Man is; the sentence allows both.

observations.quote: Where that True Phisick lyeth hid, and may be found.
observations.what: Where that True Phisick lyeth hid, and may be found
observations.note: The head numbered II.

observations.quote: that True Phisick lyeth hid
observations.note: The True Phisick is said to lie hid in a place, and to be findable there.

observations.quote: That it is to be fetcht out, and prepared truly, by fire.
observations.what: That it is to be fetcht out, and prepared truly, by fire
observations.note: The head numbered III.

observations.quote: fetcht out, and prepared truly, by fire
observations.note: Two things are done to the Phisick by fire: it is fetched out of where it lies and it is prepared; no further step is given in these lines.

observations.quote: With what vertue, and after what manner, that Phisick worketh on mans body, and expelleth his diseases.
observations.what: With what vertue, and after what manner, that Phisick worketh on mans body
observations.note: The head numbered IV: how the Phisick acts on the body.

observations.quote: What manner of Phisitian that Phisick doth require for its Minister.
observations.what: What manner of Phisitian that Phisick doth require for its Minister
observations.note: The head numbered V; the physician is called the Minister of the Phisick.

observations.quote: Of the universall and chiefe Medicine or Phisick of the most Ancient Philosophers
observations.what: the universall and chiefe Medicine or Phisick of the most Ancient Philosophers
observations.note: The head numbered VI names one Medicine as universal and chief and gives it to the most Ancient Philosophers.

observations.quote: commended of many, possessed, yea seen, or believed of very few
observations.note: This Medicine is praised by many but possessed, seen or even believed by very few.

observations.quote: Some thing in defence of the published Truth, as an Epilogue or Conclusion.
observations.what: an Epilogue or Conclusion
observations.note: A last, unnumbered head is announced: a defence of the Truth, which is called published.

voices.quote: according to the Comaedian, there can be nothing more unjust
voices.basis: the judgement is given 'according to the Comaedian'
margin note naming a writing by chapter and verse beside the passage on the vain Honours of the world; it gives no words of its own

voices.quote: See Paracels. Tom. 5. in fragm. Medicis. fol. 167, 168.
voices.basis: margin note naming a writing of Paracels. and its place

voices.quote: It is a wicked Tyranny to captivate the fancy of Students
voices.basis: runs to the end of the note after the reference to Paracels., with no verb of saying; not shown whether his words or Croll's

voices.quote: (as they call them) the Authorities and Titles of Doctorship
voices.basis: 'as they call them': the Doctors' own names for the titles

voices.quote: Galens Axioms (as he writeth) doe any more concern us
voices.basis: 'as he writeth' after 'Galens Axioms'; Galen is the only person named in the clause

voices.quote: as Socrates saith of rash Physitians, sport & play with mans skin
or rather the Image of God
voices.basis: a correction standing after Socrates's words; not shown whether his or Croll's

voices.quote: they plead in defence of their sloth and idlenesse
voices.basis: 'they plead': the physicians' plea, reported to reject it, runs to 'labours and observations'

voices.quote: One shall not repent of such a Phisitian
voices.basis: followed by a reference to Agrip:; not shown whether his words or Croll's
margin reference naming a writing of Agrip:

voices.voice: QUOTED: some of this ribble rabble
voices.basis: the opponents' verdict 'poisonous', reported in order to reject it

voices.voice: QUOTED: some of this ribble rabble
voices.basis: 'which they call': the opponents' name for the Chymists

voices.quote: Pythagoras forbids to put our victualls into a close stool
voices.basis: a prohibition given to Pythagoras by name

voices.quote: in the opinion of the wise, not to be regarded by heroike spirits
